newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-VIALBE AND DAEHLIE SHINE, YEGOROVA CHEATS.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-VIALBE AND DAEHLIE SHINE, YEGOROVA CHEATS.

text.p: Yelena Vialbe and Bjorn Daehlie left only a few crumbs to their rivals in this year's Nordic skiing world championships, which were marred by an embarrassing doping case.
Both Russian Vialbe and Nowegian Daehlie, who won five and three gold medals respectively, said they would carry on until next year's Olympics in Nagano.
This will come as bad news for the new generation, who might have to wait until the 1999 world championships in Ramsau am Dachstein, Austria, to get a chance to shine.

Lyubov Yegorova, one of the few women to contest Vialbe's supremacy over the past few years, will not be in Japan as Russian officials said she was finished in the sport after testing positive for a banned stimulant.
Worried by continuing allegations of doping in Nordic skiing, the International Ski Federation (FIS) introduced new pre-race blood tests to detect high haemoglobin levels.
But it was a routine, post-race urine test which showed Yegorova had taken a Bromantan pill.
The former world and Olympic champion admitted taking the drug, which stirred controversy at last year's Atlanta Olympics where several athletes were caught using it.
"It's sad for Nordic skiing but I'm not naive and I knew there was some doping going on," said Norwegian Trude Dybendahl-Hartz, who won silver in the relay.
"But it's comforting to see that the system put in place by FIS works and that nobody will be allowed to cheat."

Yegorova was stripped of her gold medal in the 5-km classic which went to Vialbe, allowing her to become the first woman to make a clean sweep in all races since five events were originally introduced at the world championships in 1989.
Galina Kulakova of the Soviet Union previously won all races in one championships in 1974 when only three events were contested.
But Vialbe could not be pleased with the way she earned that place in the record books.
"It will take a long time for me to forget what happened," she said. "I don't want to see Yegorova any more."
After letting Russian Alexei Prokurorov win the opening 30-km race, Daehlie showed his class by taking the next two races before helping Norway to an impressive triumph in the relay.
Cheered on by noisy fans waving Norwegian flags and shaking cowbells, Daehlie was unstoppable on his way to victories in the 10-km classic and the 15-km pursuit.
In Sunday's grand finale, the 50 kms, he was tired and had to be content with a bronze medal while Finn Mika Myllylae scored his first major win in style.
Daehlie, the most successful skier in cross-country history, hinted he might bring his career to an end after Nagano.
"I'm almost 30 and I'm starting to think of what I will do after skiing," he said, adding he was looking forward to watching his two-year-old son grow up.
Japan boosted their confidence ahead of Nagano with two world titles for Kenji Ogiwara in the Nordic combined and Masahiko Harada in the high hill ski jumping.
But Russia and Norway, who took six and four titles respectively, are still the dominant forces in the sport.
It remains to be seen whether they will still rule after Vialbe and Daehlie retire but as long as such formidable champions are still in their ranks, they have little to fear.
